analogy.p: Think of energy as money and work done as a taxi fare. The longer the journey (distance) and the higher the rate (force), the more the fare (work done) and the more money is transferred from your pocket (one energy store) into the driver's (another store). Friction is like a tax on the journey: some of your money disappears into the surroundings and cannot be spent again. The analogy breaks down because energy is never destroyed, it is only dissipated into the thermal store of the surroundings, while a fare is genuinely received by someone.

bullets: **Work done** is the energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance.
**Work done = energy transferred**, so it is measured in **joules (J)**, the same unit as energy.
Work needs both a **force** and **movement** in the direction of the force.
Pushing a wall that does not move: **no work done** (distance = 0).
Carrying a heavy bag at constant height along a flat path: the upward force is at right angles to the movement, so it does no work on the bag in the direction of motion.
Work done is a scalar quantity: it has size but no direction.
Link to other topics: energy stores and transfers (4.1), power (4.1), kinetic energy (4.1).
core.p: In physics, **work done** has a very specific meaning. When a **force** moves an object through a **distance**, the force does work on the object, and **energy is transferred**. The amount of energy transferred is exactly equal to the work done. So 'work' is not the same as effort or tiredness: if you push a wall as hard as you can and it does not move, you do no work on it, because there is no distance moved. Work done is a way of measuring how much energy a force has transferred.

bullets: **W = F s** (work done = force × distance).
W in **joules (J)**, F in **newtons (N)**, s in **metres (m)**.
Rearranged: **F = W / s** and **s = W / F**.
Doubling the force doubles the work done for the same distance.
Doubling the distance doubles the work done for the same force.
Convert units first: 250 cm = 2.5 m; 1.2 km = 1200 m.
The distance must be in the **direction of the force**.
A good exam habit: write the equation, substitute with units, then give the answer with the unit J.
core.h: The equation: work done = force × distance
core.p: The equation you need to learn and use is **work done = force × distance (moved along the line of action of the force)**. In symbols, **W = F s**, where W is work done in joules (J), F is force in newtons (N) and s is distance in metres (m). The larger the force or the further it moves the object, the more work is done and the more energy is transferred. The distance must be measured **in the direction of the force**, and you must convert centimetres or kilometres into metres before substituting.

bullets: **1 joule** is the work done when a force of **1 newton** causes a displacement of **1 metre** in the direction of the force.
The joule is the unit for work done and for all forms of energy.
Raising a 1 N weight through 1 m needs 1 J.
A slightly different unit, the newton-metre, is also used for moments, but there it is not a joule because the distance is perpendicular to the force.
Quote the definition in full: force, 1 newton, displacement 1 metre, in the direction of the force.
core.p: The spec says one joule is the work done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre in the direction of the force. This follows directly from W = F s: 1 N × 1 m = 1 N m, so **1 joule = 1 newton-metre**. It is a small amount of energy. Lifting a 100 g apple (weight about 1 N) by 1 m does about 1 J of work. Learning this definition gives easy marks in short-answer questions.

bullets: Pushing a box: chemical store (muscles) to kinetic store (box) and thermal store (friction).
Lifting an object: energy transferred to the **gravitational potential energy store**.
Stretching a spring: energy transferred to the **elastic potential energy store**.
Accelerating a car: work done by the engine force increases the **kinetic energy store**.
Energy is **conserved**: total energy in = total energy out, although some is dissipated.
Work done = energy transferred, so **work done in joules = change in energy in joules**.
Link: **gravitational potential energy = m g h**, which equals the work done lifting at constant speed.
core.p: Work done is the **process** by which energy moves from one store to another through a force. When you push a trolley, energy is transferred from the chemical store in your muscles to the kinetic store of the trolley. The energy transferred equals the work done. Whenever work is done, you should ask: where did the energy come from, and where did it end up? This is the reasoning examiners look for, not just the calculation.

bullets: Work done **against frictional forces** causes the temperature of the object and the surroundings to rise.
Energy is transferred to the **thermal energy store** by heating.
This energy is **dissipated**: it spreads out into the surroundings and is wasted.
Examples: brakes on a bicycle, rubbing hands, a meteor entering the atmosphere, a sliding box.
Reducing friction (lubrication, smoother surfaces) reduces wasted energy.
Friction acts **opposite to the motion**, so the work done by friction is a loss from the kinetic store.
Link: this is why efficiency of machines is always less than 100%.
core.p: When an object is moved against a **frictional force**, the work done by the applied force does not all end up as useful energy. Much of it is **dissipated as heat**: the surfaces rub together, their particles vibrate faster, and the **temperature of the object and the surroundings rises**. This is why rubbing your hands together makes them warm, and why brake discs get hot. The energy transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings is spread out and is not usefully recoverable.

bullets: Constant speed: **pushing force = friction**, resultant force = 0.
All the work done goes to the **thermal store** (no change in kinetic energy).
Pushing force greater than friction: the box accelerates and gains kinetic energy.
Work done by friction on the box is **negative** (it removes energy from the box).
Doubling the distance pushed doubles the energy dissipated.
Heavier box: normal contact force is bigger, so friction is bigger, so more work is needed over the same distance.
Link to Newton's first and second laws.
core.h: Constant speed: work done equals energy dissipated
core.p: If you push a box along a rough floor at **constant speed**, the resultant force on it is zero, so your pushing force equals the friction force. You are still doing work (force × distance), but the box's kinetic energy does not change, so all the energy you transfer ends up as **thermal energy** through friction. If you push with a bigger force than friction, the extra resultant force accelerates the box and some of the work increases its kinetic energy.

bullets: Step 1: write the equation **W = F s**.
Step 2: convert units (cm to m, kg to N using weight = m g).
Step 3: substitute and calculate.
Step 4: give the answer with the unit **J** (or kJ).
If lifting at constant speed, the force equals the **weight** of the object.
If given the energy transferred, that is the work done.
Check the answer is sensible: a small force over a small distance should give a small number of joules.
Quote significant figures consistent with the data.
core.p: Work done calculations follow a fixed pattern that earns full marks. First, identify the force that is doing the work and check it acts in the direction of the movement. Second, convert all units into newtons and metres. Third, write W = F s, substitute the numbers, and give the answer in joules. If the question gives the work done and asks for a force or distance, rearrange first. Lifting questions need weight first, using W = m g, where g is 9.8 N/kg on Earth.

bullets: Axes: force (N) on the y-axis, displacement (m) on the x-axis.
**Area under the graph = work done** (in J).
Constant force: the area is a rectangle, area = F × s.
Spring obeying Hooke's law: triangle, area = 1/2 × F × e.
Read values carefully from the axes and use the right units.
If the graph is a curve, count squares to estimate the area.
The idea is not directly named in the specification statement but supports the equation.
core.p: When force is plotted against distance moved, the **area under the graph** equals the work done. For a constant force this area is a rectangle: height F, width s, so area = F s, which matches the equation. This idea is useful when the force changes, for example stretching a spring where force increases with extension: the area under the line (a triangle) gives the work done, equal to the elastic energy stored.

bullets: Work done by brakes = **kinetic energy lost**: F s = 1/2 m v².
Braking distance **s = (1/2 m v²) / F**.
Double the speed: kinetic energy ×4, braking distance ×4 (for the same force).
Brakes and tyres **get hot** because kinetic energy is transferred to the thermal store.
A bigger braking force gives a shorter braking distance.
Worn brakes or wet roads give smaller braking forces and longer distances.
Link to stopping distances.
core.h: Links to kinetic energy and braking
core.p: A moving car has **kinetic energy**, calculated with Ek = 1/2 m v². To stop it, the brakes apply a force over a distance, and the **work done by the braking force equals the kinetic energy lost**. This work is transferred to the thermal stores of the brakes, tyres, road and air. This explains why braking distance depends on speed squared: doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy, so the work needed (force × distance) is four times bigger for the same braking force.

bullets: **P = W / t** (power = work done ÷ time).
1 watt = 1 joule per second.
Rearranged: W = P t and t = W / P.
A 60 W motor does 60 J of work every second.
Two people lift the same box to the same height: the quicker one has more power, same work.
Time must be in **seconds**.
Power is also energy transferred / time, because work done = energy transferred.
core.p: Work done is linked to **power**, which is the rate at which energy is transferred, or the rate of doing work. The equation is **power = work done / time**, P = W / t, with power in watts (W), work in joules (J) and time in seconds (s). One watt is one joule per second. A powerful motor does the same work in a shorter time. Do not confuse the symbol W for work with the unit W for watts.

bullets: Crane lifts a load: work done = weight × height = gain in gravitational potential energy.
Person pushes a car: chemical store to kinetic store and thermal store.
Skidding tyres: kinetic energy to thermal energy in tyres and road.
A meteor in the atmosphere: work done against air resistance heats the meteor.
Pumping a bicycle pump: work done compressing air makes the pump warm.
Always name the energy stores: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical.
State clearly that **work done = energy transferred**.
core.p: Examiners test this topic with short calculations and with explanations about energy. Common contexts are pushing or pulling objects, lifting loads with cranes or people, cars braking, and friction heating. In explain questions, always connect three ideas: a **force** moves through a **distance**, **work is done**, and **energy is transferred** (to a named store). Adding the word 'dissipated' when the energy is wasted by friction is often what earns the final mark.

bullets: Pushing a wall that does not move: s = 0, so W = F × 0 = **0 J**.
Carrying a bag at constant height along a level path: the supporting force acts upwards but the movement is horizontal, so that force does **no work** on the bag.
A weight lifted upwards at constant speed: the lifting force acts along the movement, so work done = weight × height.
A force acting opposite to the movement (friction on a sliding box) removes energy from the moving object.
Quote the reason in full: 'there is no movement in the direction of the force'.
If the object moves but not along the line of the force, only the **distance in the direction of the force** is used in W = F s.
Exam phrase: work done is the **energy transferred** by a force, not how hard something feels.
core.h: When is work done and when is it not? (reasoning questions)
core.p: Examiners like to test whether you understand that work done needs a force and movement in the direction of that force. If an object does not move, the distance moved is zero, so the work done is zero however large the force is. If the force acts at right angles to the movement, the force does not transfer energy to the object, so no work is done by that force. In everyday language 'work' means effort, but in physics it is the energy transferred by a force, so a tired person pushing a fixed wall does no work on the wall. Use the idea W = F s and state clearly which force you are talking about.

bullets: Convert **cm to m** by dividing by 100 and **km to m** by multiplying by 1000.
Convert a mass to a force with **weight = m g** (g = 9.8 N/kg unless given another value).
W = F s: if the force is in kN, convert to N first (1 kN = 1000 N).
Show the substitution line, for example **W = 35 × 8.0**, to pick up the method mark even if the arithmetic slips.
Give the answer to a suitable number of significant figures, usually the same as the data.
Unit check: N × m = J, so no extra conversion is needed once SI units are used.
core.p: Work done is always measured in joules, and the joule can be written as a newton metre because 1 J = 1 N × 1 m. Large amounts of work are often quoted in kilojoules (kJ) or megajoules (MJ), so you must convert before substituting into the equation. Distances must be in metres and forces in newtons, otherwise the answer will be wrong by a factor of 10, 100 or 1000. After calculating, check that the size of the answer is sensible for the situation and that you have included the unit with the final line of your working.

exam: **'State the equation'** (1 mark): work done = force × distance (moved along the line of action of the force).
**'Calculate the work done'** (2 marks): 1 mark for substitution into W = F s, 1 mark for the answer with unit J.
**'Define the joule'** (1 to 2 marks): one newton, one metre, in the direction of the force.
**'Explain why the brakes get hot'** (2 to 3 marks): work is done against friction, kinetic energy is transferred to the thermal store, so temperature increases.
**'Describe the energy transfer'** (2 marks): name the store the energy comes from and the store it goes to.
Always write the **units** and convert to **N and m** first; mark schemes penalise missing units.
For **rearranging** (2 to 3 marks): s = W / F or F = W / s, then substitute.
For lifting questions, find **weight = m g** first (g = 9.8 N/kg unless told otherwise).
**4 and 6 mark** answers: link force, distance, work done, energy store changes, and dissipation, in a logical order.
Use the key phrase **'dissipated to the surroundings'** for wasted energy.
If a graph of force against distance is given, use **area under the graph** for work done.
Check answers for sense: a large car braking force over several metres should give thousands of joules.

mistakes.r: Work done is the energy transferred by a force moving an object through a distance (W = F s).
mistakes.w: Work done is how tired you are or how hard you try.

mistakes.r: Work done is measured in joules (J). Watts (W) are the unit of power.
mistakes.w: Using the wrong unit for work, such as N or W.

mistakes.r: Distance must be in metres before using W = F s.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert cm or km to metres.

mistakes.r: Calculate the weight first: W = m g (N), then work done = weight × height.
mistakes.w: Using mass instead of weight for the force when lifting.

mistakes.r: Energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings; total energy is conserved.
mistakes.w: Saying energy is 'used up' or 'lost' in friction.

mistakes.r: If there is no movement in the direction of the force, no work is done.
mistakes.w: Saying a force that does not move an object does work.

mistakes.r: One joule is the work done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre in the direction of the force.
mistakes.w: Defining the joule without 'in the direction of the force'.

mistakes.r: Work done against friction raises the temperature of the object and the surroundings.
mistakes.w: Writing 'friction makes heat' without stating what is heated.

mistakes.r: Check units: J for work done, W for power.
mistakes.w: Mixing up W for work and W for watts.

mistakes.r: If the force is at right angles to the movement, that force does no work.
mistakes.w: A force always does work if it is large enough.

summary: You must know that when a force makes an object move through a distance, the force does work and energy is transferred. You must be able to calculate work done using W = F s, state that one joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre in the direction of the force, and explain that work done against friction heats the object and its surroundings. It matters because work done links forces to energy, and explains braking, lifting, pushing and why moving surfaces get hot.

terms.d: The energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance.
The unit of work and energy. 1 J is the work done when a force of 1 N causes a displacement of 1 m in the direction of the force.
A push or pull on an object, measured in newtons (N).
The distance moved in a particular direction, measured in metres (m).
The movement of energy from one store to another.
Energy that is spread out into the surroundings, usually by heating, and not usefully recovered.
A force that opposes the motion of surfaces sliding over each other, causing work to be done against it.
The store of energy in the vibrating particles of a substance; increases when temperature rises.
The energy an object has due to its motion, Ek = 1/2 m v².
The energy an object has due to its height in a gravitational field, Ep = m g h.
The rate of energy transfer or the rate of doing work, P = W / t, in watts (W).
The unit of power; 1 W = 1 joule per second.
The force of gravity on an object, W = m g, in newtons.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores.
The single force with the same effect as all the forces acting on an object.
The straight line along which a force acts; only movement along this line counts in W = F s.
Unit of work done when force is in newtons and distance in metres; 1 N m = 1 J.
1000 joules, used for larger amounts of work or energy.
Energy transferred to the thermal store of the object and surroundings when a force moves an object against friction.

worked.q: A student pushes a box with a constant force of 35 N for 8.0 m along the floor. Calculate the work done. (2 marks)
A 4.0 kg crate is lifted at a constant speed through 2.5 m. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the work done. (3 marks)
steps: At constant speed the lifting force equals the weight, 39.2 N.

worked.q: A car of mass 1000 kg travelling at 20 m/s brakes with a constant force of 5000 N until it stops. Calculate the braking distance. (4 marks)
steps: Work done by brakes = kinetic energy lost = 200 000 J.
